catalog_locator: Front matter, 'Explicaciones', second page (PDF p. 8 of the SIL scan; pages unnumbered)
catalog_quote: En palabras polisílabas, la acentuación se encuentra por lo general en la segunda sílaba. Sólo se lo escribe cuando difiere del patrón predominante. El empleo de guión indica que las dos vocales de la secuencia así separadas funcionan como núcleos de sílabas diferentes.
sweep_summary: All three sweep items are one work: Pitman & Pitman, 'Araona syllable and stress' (written Nov. 1976, issued in the SIL Riberalta Work Papers 1972-1976, April 1978; Glottolog refs 45185, 697624, 52115 are duplicates, the last with a garbled author field). It is the dedicated first-hand study and was already on file (fetched sources 2026-09-13 via Wayback from SIL archives item 10842; I copied it, its scanned and verified page images into and wrote. It REFINES the catalog: the 'normal' pattern is the second syllable of the word counted from the left edge with CV prefixes included (confirming the catalog default and the 1981 dictionary note, which is a one-line summary of this paper), but (a) disyllables are initial-stressed in isolation, (b) initial stress is the productive exponent of a deleted e- prefix on C-initial polysyllabic nouns/verbs, with surface minimal pairs (bákʷa/bakʷá, bána/baná), (c) monosyllabic verb root + short TAM suffix takes initial stress, (d) a closed list of unexplained initial-stress nouns; the authors conclude 'Stress is predictable except when indicating presence of noun prefix obligatory possession and verb prefix affirmative'. The catalog's 'fixed-unreviewed' label should carry this morphological caveat (second-syllable default with a grammatically conditioned initial-stress alternative). Two extra first-hand sources were read as well: Pitman & Pitman 1970 (archive. Tallman 2024 (on file) confirms the second-syllable default instrumentally, reanalysed as a post-lexical L+H* pitch accent on the second syllable of a domain whose left edge is the prefix slot, and disputes the Pitmans' exceptions. Best new statement: Pitman & Pitman 1978 sec. 2.2/2.6/4, which supersedes the catalog's deciding source (the 1981 dictionary front-matter note). Still unobtained: Emkow 2006/2019 'A grammar of Araona' (stress analysis at 86ff per Guillaume forthc.; no open copy; not a sweep item). sil.org and HathiTrust are Cloudflare-gated, language-archives.org refused connections, Wayback CDX was offline, Google Books API returned no hits.

new_statements.reading: Default word stress on the second syllable counted from the left edge of the word with CV prefixes included (pakʷáebo), so the catalog's second-syllable, left-edge, weight-insensitive coding is the right default. But the source itself does not describe a strictly fixed system: (i) disyllabic nouns (and e-nouns) are initial-stressed in isolation and second-stressed in connected speech; (ii) a productive class of C-initial polysyllabic nouns and verbs carries initial stress as the sole exponent of a deleted e- prefix, giving surface minimal pairs (bákʷa 'child' / bakʷá 'snake'; bána 'aff.-plant' / baná 'plant'); (iii) monosyllabic root + short TAM suffix is initial-stressed; (iv) a closed list of unexplained initial-stress nouns. The authors' own summary is 'predictable except when indicating presence of' the two e- prefixes, i.e. second-syllable default with a morphologically conditioned initial-stress alternative. Tallman 2024 (pitch tracks) confirms the second-syllable default of the domain and reinterprets it as a post-lexical L+H* pitch accent.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim on the held page image (dictionary front matter, PDF p. 8) and independently in two other held Pitman sources (1976/78 stress paper sec. 2.2; Bosquejo 1980: 74-75). (2) The record's deciding citation is dictionary front matter (1981), formally a weak kind, but the same claim is made in a dedicated SIL stress paper we hold, and the modern instrumental study fetched sources now (Tallman 2024: 548, 573, LangSci open access) states that the L+H* accent is predictable and docks by default on the second syllable of its domain, 'agreeing... superficially' with the Pitmans' rule while disputing their exceptions. So the fixed peninitial coding (01 010 0100...) is confirmed by the best modern source; nothing seen suggests a recode. Two refinements worth noting in the record rather than recoding: Pitman & Pitman 1976 sec. 2.2-2.3 say disyllabic nouns 'in isolation' are stresse

sources.citation: Pitman, Donald & Mary Pitman (1970). La jerarquía fonológica de araona. Notas Lingüísticas de Bolivia 8. Riberalta: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano. 18 pp. (Rosetta Project excerpt pp. 1-13)
sources.quote: El núcleo de la palabra se indica por una acentuación fuerte, la cual contrasta fonémicamente: áno abuela / ané doloroso; adóe profundo / ákoi árbol; sátani rajando / samáne ¡rájalo! [...] La palabra contiene sólo una acentuación fuerte. Esta acentuación se encuentra por lo general en la primera sílaba dentro de las palabras que consisten de sólo dos sílabas, y se encuentra en la segunda sílaba dentro de las palabras que contienen más de dos sílabas. En las palabras que contienen más de tres sílabas, una acentuación suave ocurre por lo general sílaba por medio, saliendo del núcleo. (pp. 9-10) [The word nucleus is marked by a strong accent, which contrasts phonemically ... The word has only one strong accent. It generally falls on the first syllable in words of only two syllables, and on the second syllable in words of more than two syllables. In words of more than three syllables a weak accent generally occurs on every other syllable outward from the nucleus.]
sources.locator: sec. 3 'La palabra fonológica', pp. 9-10 (read on the page images)
sources.note: Earlier (pre-1976) first-hand phonology by the same authors: disyllables initial, longer words second syllable, one strong accent per word, alternating secondary accent, and stress said to 'contrast phonemically' (the pairs given are mostly disyllable-vs-trisyllable, i.e. explained by the length rule). Word nucleus cued by loudness, high pitch and length; phrase stress may 'disturb' word stress (p. 10). Superseded by the authors' own 1976 paper, which restates the disyllable facts as an isolation effect and derives the initial-stress class from e- deletion.
